newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Yeltsin comes to Ukraine to sign friendship treaty.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin comes to Ukraine to sign friendship treaty.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin began a long-delayed state visit to Kiev on Friday to sign a friendship pact with Ukraine and end what many diplomatic analysts saw as a "cold war" between the two Slav states.
"I am stepping on this hospitable land with a feeling of great excitement and hope," Yeltsin told reporters on arrival.
Yeltsin promised before leaving Moscow that "in extreme situations" Moscow would defend Ukraine -- which has been seeking security guarantees from the NATO defence alliance.

"This is in the agreement, that we will participate together to defend Ukraine if anything happens," Yeltsin said in an interview to be broadcast later on Ukrainian television Studio 1+1 and Russian public television.
Ukraine has never turned to Russia for security protection since it gained independence in 1991 and some circles in Kiev see Moscow as a threat rather than a brotherly Slav state.

Russia opposes North Atlantic Treaty Organisation's plans to admit new members in eastern Europe and fears Ukraine, which is trying to free itself from centuries of Moscow domination, could seek membership itself.
Yeltsin on Wednesday signed a pact giving Moscow some say in the alliance in return for unspoken assent to NATO's plans to admit eastern European countries from the former Warsaw pact.

But the Kremlin stressed it would not tolerate former Soviet republics joining, and on Thursday Ukraine tacitly accepted it would not seek NATO membership by initialling a security pact with the Western alliance in the Portugese town of Sintra.

Yeltsin and President Leonid Kuchma are due to sign a friendship treaty on Saturday which was first drawn up two years ago and has mostly been delayed by arguing over the former Soviet Black Sea Fleet based at Ukraine's Crimean peninsula, Ukraine's energy debt and the fate of Soviet nuclear missiles.
"There are many knots in our relations which sour our life and cooperation. We must cut these knots," Yeltsin, who was later to be formally welcomed by President Leonid Kuchma, said.
"(It is) the most difficult visit and the most important foreign policy act by the Russian president in 1997," Interfax quoted Yeltsin's spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky as saying.

Ukrainian Prime Minister Pavlo Lazarenko and Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin met in Kiev on Wednesday and signed a series of deals they said settled all bilateral problems ahead of the summit, including the shareout of the Black Sea Fleet.
Russia won a 20-year lease to keep its share of the rusting naval force at the Crimean naval base of Sevastopol.
Moscow and Kiev, which played crucial roles in ending the Soviet Union in late 1991, have since been caught in a web of mutual recriminations over the heritage of the communist empire.

"Yeltsin's visit to Kiev and massive talks held ahead of it herald a broad political agreement which is expected to take away the huge strains of the undeclared cold war between two former 'sister-republics'," the Ukraina Moloda daily wrote.
The draft friendship treaty has not been released, but Russia's Nezavisimaya Gazeta published parts of it on Friday.
"(Russia and Ukraine) respect each other's territorial integrity and confirm that the existing border between them cannot be changed," the treaty said without elaboration.

Russia's nationalists have urged the Kremlin to question Ukraine's right to Crimea, the Russian-populated Black Sea region handed over in a largely symbolic gesture by the Soviet leadership in the 1950s from Russia to Ukraine.
"Each side will not take part or support steps aimed at the other party and promises not to strike deals with third parties aimed at the other partner," one clause said.
